error_modes.label: Altitude control in the tactical block

texts.0: SP, due to a lookout that stayed locked on No1 with no altimeter sample during the tactical turns, did not maintain the briefed tactical altitude. The aircraft climbed more than 1000 feet above and later descended more than 500 feet below the briefed block, exceeding the code 1 tolerance in both directions. The IP had to direct the climb back into the block and take control of the power setting to stop the descent.
texts.1: SP, due to an altitude cross-check that was resumed only after each rollout, did not hold the briefed tactical altitude while converting energy in the turns. Deviation reached +1000 feet on the energy-gaining side and -500 feet after the reversal, exactly at the code 1 tolerance. Return to the block came only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and with noticeable delay.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction as the nose came down through the horizon in the tactical turn, did not keep altitude within the tight tolerance. Deviation grew to about +700 feet and, on the following reversal, to about -400 feet, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP recognized the trend on the altimeter and re-established the block within a few seconds without any prompt or intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude throughout the navigation legs and the tactical turns, holding within +500 / -300 feet, that is inside the code 3 tolerance. Power and pitch were adjusted before the deviation developed, so corrections stayed small and continuous. Altitude sampling was interleaved with the lookout on No1 without either being dropped.
texts.4: SP held the briefed tactical altitude within approximately 100 feet through every turn and reversal, with negligible excursions even during the energy exchange. Pitch and power were pre-empted rather than corrected, so the altitude trace remained flat. The altimeter sample was fitted into the lookout cycle without any pause in visual contact with No1.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the altitude tolerance but used nearly the full allowance on the low side, settling toward -300 feet each time bank was increased. The deviation was always caught and corrected, yet the same downward trend repeated on successive turns. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch requirement at the roll-in and hold the block within 200 feet.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude, holding the deviation to about +900 / -480 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the altimeter sample being taken only as the lookout returned to No1 rather than interleaved with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to interleave the altimeter sample with the lookout cycle, not only as it returns to No1.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude, holding the deviation to about +700 / -400 feet, due to the power reduction as the nose came through the horizon being applied a beat after the pitch change rather than with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the power reduction with the pitch change, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude, holding the deviation to about +450 / -280 feet, due to the correction at bank increase being applied a fraction after the trend appeared rather than as it began. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to correct at the first sign of the trend, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude throughout the navigation legs and the tactical turns, holding to about +700 / -400 feet, power and pitch adjusted before the deviation developed with altitude sampling interleaved with the lookout on No1. Correcting at the first sign of the trend, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the block further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed tactical altitude to about +450 / -280 feet through every turn and reversal, inside the code 3 tolerance, pitch and power pre-empted rather than corrected with the altitude trace remaining flat. The only refinement available was to hold that same anticipation through the steepest reversal of the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed tactical altitude within approximately 100 feet through every turn and reversal, with negligible excursions even during the energy exchange, the altimeter sample fitted into the lookout cycle without any pause in visual contact with No1. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude-anticipation discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to power handling that lagged the flight-path change at entry and exit of the tactical turns, did not maintain the briefed entry and exit airspeed. Airspeed varied by more than 30 knots from the briefed value, exceeding the code 1 tolerance, and decayed low enough to leave no energy for the following reversal. The IP had to command the power setting and unload the aircraft to restore the briefed speed.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed power setting carried through the entry regardless of the bank applied, did not hold the briefed entry and exit airspeed. Deviation reached 30 knots from the briefed value, that is the code 1 tolerance, on both the entry and the exit. SP restored speed only after the IP called it out, and the correction was applied late in the turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a power increase begun after the bank was already established rather than with it, did not keep airspeed tight at the entry of the tactical turns. Deviation reached about 20 knots below the briefed value, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP identified the shortfall from the airspeed indicator and restored the briefed speed before the rollout without prompting.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed within 15 knots throughout the tactical turns, inside the code 3 tolerance. Power was matched to the bank and the pitch attitude as the turn was entered, so no large corrections were required. Exit speed was set early enough to support the next maneuver.
texts.4: SP held entry and exit airspeed within a few knots of the briefed value on every turn, with negligible variation across the sortie. Power was led into the maneuver so the airspeed indicator stayed essentially steady through the reversal. Energy at each rollout was exactly what the following maneuver required.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the airspeed tolerance but consistently exited the tactical turns on the slow side of the briefed value, using most of the allowance each time. Speed was always recovered on the following leg, yet the same slow bias reappeared at every exit. SP is expected to add power earlier at the roll-in and hold the exit speed within 10 knots.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 28 knots, at the edge of the standard, due to the power increase at roll-in being added a beat after the bank was established rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add power with the bank at roll-in, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 21 knots, due to the power step at exit being matched to the pitch attitude a fraction after the bank came out rather than with it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to match the power step to the pitch attitude as the bank comes out, not after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 13 knots, due to the exit speed being confirmed a fraction after the rollout rather than through it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm exit speed through the rollout, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed within about 20 knots throughout the tactical turns, inside the code 3 tolerance, power matched to the bank and pitch attitude as the turn was entered with no large corrections required. Confirming exit speed through the rollout itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound entry-exit-airspeed discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed within about 13 knots on every turn, exit speed set early enough to support the next maneuver. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead through the fastest reversal of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed entry-exit-airspeed discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held entry and exit airspeed within a few knots of the briefed value on every turn, with negligible variation across the sortie, power led into the maneuver so the airspeed indicator stayed essentially steady through the reversal with energy at each rollout exactly what the following maneuver required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional entry-exit-airspeed discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a rollout started from the aircraft attitude alone with no reference to the required recovery heading, did not roll out in the tactical formation position. The heading error exceeded 30 degrees from the briefed recovery heading, beyond the code 1 tolerance, and the formation geometry could not be rebuilt from that position. The IP had to give the heading to steer and direct the correction back toward line abreast.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead point for the rollout that was not computed for the bank being flown, did not roll out on the required recovery heading. The error reached 30 degrees, that is the code 1 tolerance, and the resulting geometry left No2 well out of position. SP corrected only after the IP stated the heading, and the correction was slow enough that the next turn was entered off-heading.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout begun slightly late for the rate of turn being flown, did not roll out precisely on the recovery heading. The error was about 20 degrees, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP saw the discrepancy on the HSI, adjusted heading promptly and re-established the tactical position without any intervention.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading within 10 degrees after each tactical turn, inside the code 3 tolerance. The lead point was adjusted for the bank flown, so the rollout arrived on heading rather than being corrected after it. The formation position was re-established directly from the rollout.
texts.4: SP rolled out within a couple of degrees of the required recovery heading on every tactical turn, with negligible correction after the wings were level. The lead point was anticipated for each rate of turn, so no post-rollout heading chasing was needed. The tactical position was regained as the rollout completed.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out inside the heading tolerance but consistently overshot in the same direction, using most of the allowance on every turn in that direction. The error was recognized and taken out each time, though only after the wings were level. SP is expected to lead the rollout earlier and arrive on the recovery heading within 5 degrees.

texts_at.1: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading, holding the error to about 28 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the lead point for the rollout being computed for a shallower bank than the one actually flown. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to compute the lead point for the bank actually flown, not a shallower one.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading, holding the error to about 19 degrees, due to the rollout being begun a beat later than the rate of turn called for. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to begin the rollout exactly when the rate of turn calls for it, not a beat later.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading, holding the error to about 9 degrees, due to the heading being confirmed on the HSI a fraction after the wings levelled rather than through the rollout. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the heading through the rollout itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading within about 19 degrees after each tactical turn, inside the code 3 tolerance, the lead point adjusted for the bank flown so the rollout arrived on heading rather than being corrected after it. Confirming the heading through the rollout itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid rollout-lead discipline.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the required recovery heading within about 9 degrees on each turn, the formation position re-established directly from the rollout. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead through the sharpest reversal of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed rollout-lead discipline.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out within a couple of degrees of the required recovery heading on every tactical turn, with negligible correction after the wings were level, the lead point anticipated for each rate of turn so no post-rollout heading chasing was needed with the tactical position regained as the rollout completed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding rollout-lead discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to abrupt stick inputs used to chase the leader instead of a steady pull, did not maintain the briefed continuous G during the tactical turns. G varied by more than 1.0 from the briefed value, exceeding the code 1 tolerance, with a light-G excursion followed by a rapid pull that produced buffet. The IP had to take control of the pull to stabilize the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a pull that was relaxed each time visual contact with No1 was regained, did not hold continuous G through the turn. The variation reached 1.0 G from the briefed value, that is the code 1 tolerance, and the turn rate changed noticeably within the maneuver. SP steadied the pull only after the IP called for a constant G, and the correction was applied late in the turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a pull applied progressively rather than set at the roll-in, did not keep the G steady through the first part of the tactical turn. The variation was about 0.7 G from the briefed value, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP felt the change in turn rate, stabilized the pull and completed the remainder of the turn at the briefed G without intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained continuous G within 0.5 of the briefed value throughout the tactical turns, inside the code 3 tolerance. The pull was set at the roll-in and held steady, so turn rate and radius stayed predictable for No1. Energy was converted at the planned rate with no unloading during the turn.
texts.4: SP held the briefed continuous G with negligible variation across every turn, the stick force staying essentially constant from roll-in to rollout. Turn rate and radius were repeatable, which kept the formation geometry stable without further correction. No unloading or abrupt reloading occurred while the lookout shifted between No1 and the horizon.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the G tolerance but the pull drifted low in the second half of each turn, using most of the allowance before being restored. The G was always brought back to the briefed value, yet the same relaxation repeated turn after turn. SP is expected to hold the set stick force throughout the maneuver and keep the variation within 0.3 G.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed continuous G, holding the variation to about 0.88 G, at the edge of the standard, due to the stick force relaxing in the second half of the turn before it was restored. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to hold the stick force set through the whole turn, not relax it partway.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed continuous G, holding the variation to about 0.65 G, due to the pull being applied progressively rather than set at the roll-in. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the pull at the roll-in, not build it progressively.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed continuous G, holding the variation to about 0.4 G, due to the stick force settling a fraction after the roll-in rather than at it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to settle the stick force exactly at the roll-in, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP maintained continuous G within about 0.65 of the briefed value throughout the tactical turns, inside the code 3 tolerance, the pull set at the roll-in and held steady so turn rate and radius stayed predictable for No1. Settling the stick force exactly at the roll-in, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the hold further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady continuous-G discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained continuous G within about 0.4 of the briefed value on every turn, energy converted at the planned rate with no unloading during the turn. The only refinement available was to hold that same setting through the longest turn of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate continuous-G discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed continuous G with negligible variation across every turn, the stick force staying essentially constant from roll-in to rollout, turn rate and radius repeatable which kept the formation geometry stable without further correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary continuous-G discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a position assessment based on the size of No1 rather than on the bearing line, did not maintain the tactical line abreast position. The bearing deviation exceeded 30 degrees, beyond the code 1 tolerance, with the aircraft sustained well aft of line abreast and unable to support the formation. The IP had to direct the power and heading corrections needed to rebuild the position.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections that were applied only after the bearing error had become obvious, did not hold the tactical line abreast position. The deviation reached 30 degrees aft of the briefed bearing, that is the code 1 tolerance. SP moved back up the bearing line only after the IP prompted the correction, and the recovery took most of the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a power correction that was smaller than the closure required, did not keep the bearing tight after the tactical turn. The deviation reached about 20 degrees from line abreast, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP recognized the aft position against the canopy reference, applied the required power and re-established the bearing before the next turn without intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position within 10 degrees of the briefed bearing, inside the code 3 tolerance. Small power and heading corrections were applied as soon as the bearing started to change, so the position never developed a large error. The formation stayed mutually supporting throughout the navigation route.
texts.4: SP held the line abreast bearing within a few degrees for the whole sortie, including through the reversals, with negligible excursions. Corrections were anticipated from the leader's turn rate rather than applied after the error appeared. The bearing line was maintained without any visible power chasing.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the bearing tolerance but sat persistently on the aft side of line abreast, using most of the allowance on each leg. The position was recoverable and was corrected when called for, though the same aft bias returned after every turn. SP is expected to correct the bearing at first indication and hold the position within 5 degrees.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position, holding the bearing deviation to about 28 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the power correction after each turn being sized smaller than the closure required. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size the power correction to the closure required, not smaller.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position, holding the bearing deviation to about 19 degrees, due to the aft position being recognized against the canopy reference a beat after it developed rather than as it developed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recognize the aft position against the canopy reference as it develops, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position, holding the bearing deviation to about 9 degrees, due to the bearing being re-established a fraction after the correction rather than in the same motion. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to re-establish the bearing in the same motion as the correction.

texts_above.2: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position within about 19 degrees of the briefed bearing, inside the code 3 tolerance, small power and heading corrections applied as soon as the bearing started to change so the position never developed a large error. Re-establishing the bearing in the same motion as the correction, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the position further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable line-abreast discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the tactical line abreast position within about 9 degrees of the briefed bearing on every leg, the formation staying mutually supporting throughout the navigation route. The only refinement available was to hold that same correction speed through the fastest reversal of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good line-abreast discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the line abreast bearing within a few degrees for the whole sortie, including through the reversals, with negligible excursions, corrections anticipated from the leader's turn rate rather than applied after the error appeared with the bearing line maintained without any visible power chasing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior line-abreast discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a lateral spacing judged only from the apparent size of No1 with no cross-check against ground references, did not maintain the briefed lateral separation. The error exceeded 1000 feet, beyond the code 1 tolerance, closing to a spacing that removed the maneuvering room required for the tactical turns. The IP had to direct a heading change away from the leader to restore safe separation.
texts.1: SP, due to heading corrections toward No1 that were not removed once the bearing was regained, did not hold the briefed lateral separation. The error reached 1000 feet, that is the code 1 tolerance, with the formation alternately compressed and stretched between turns. SP re-established the briefed spacing only after the IP called it, and the correction was delayed into the following turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly excessive heading correction applied to regain the bearing, did not keep lateral separation tight after the reversal. The error grew to about 700 feet, that is between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP identified the change in spacing against the ground background, took out the excess heading and restored the briefed separation without any prompting.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation within 500 feet throughout the tactical legs and the turns, inside the code 3 tolerance. Heading corrections were small and were removed as soon as the spacing was regained, so the formation width stayed constant. Separation supported both the lookout responsibilities and the maneuvering room needed for the turns.
texts.4: SP held the briefed lateral separation with negligible variation across the whole route, including through the tactical turns. Spacing was assessed against ground references as well as the leader, so the formation width was maintained without cyclic compression. The geometry gave full maneuvering room at every reversal.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the lateral separation tolerance but flew consistently on the close side, using most of the allowance during and after each turn. The spacing was safe and was opened when required, yet the tendency to close reappeared at every reversal. SP is expected to set the correction earlier in the turn and hold separation within 300 feet.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 900 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the heading correction toward No1 being removed a beat after the bearing was regained rather than as it was regained. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to remove the heading correction as the bearing is regained, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 680 feet, due to the excess heading correction being taken out a fraction after the reversal rather than through it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to take out the excess heading correction through the reversal, not a fraction after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 400 feet, due to the spacing being cross-checked against a ground reference a fraction after No1 rather than together with No1. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to cross-check spacing against a ground reference together with No1, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation within about 680 feet throughout the tactical legs and the turns, inside the code 3 tolerance, heading corrections small and removed as soon as the spacing was regained so the formation width stayed constant. Cross-checking spacing against a ground reference together with No1, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured lateral-separation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed lateral separation within about 400 feet throughout the tactical legs, the geometry giving full maneuvering room at every reversal. The only refinement available was to hold that same cross-check through the tightest reversal of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise lateral-separation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed lateral separation with negligible variation across the whole route, including through the tactical turns, spacing assessed against ground references as well as the leader so the formation width was maintained without cyclic compression. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate lateral-separation discipline.

error_modes.label: Clearing and responsibility airspace as No2

texts.0: SP, due to an unagreed division of lookout responsibility within the formation, did not execute clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 during the tactical turns. The area into which the formation turned was left uncleared and terrain clearance over the high ground was not assessed, so the safe maneuvering altitude was not ensured. The IP had to clear the turn and direct a climb before the maneuver could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout scan that remained on No1 with no coverage of the assigned sector, did not clear the responsibility airspace before the tactical turns. Clearing was performed only after the IP called for it, and terrain clearance for maneuvering over the ridge was confirmed late. The formation entered the turn before the check of the assigned sector was complete.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan cycle that gave too much time to the leader, did not clear the full responsibility airspace at the start of each turn. The sector away from No1 received only a partial check on the first reversal. SP noticed the omission, extended the scan to cover the assigned airspace and confirmed safe maneuvering altitude over the high ground before the following turn, without prompting.
texts.3: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 before and during each tactical turn, according to the relative position in the formation. The scan was cycled between No1, the sector of responsibility and the terrain ahead, so both traffic and safe maneuvering altitude over the high ground were confirmed. No clearing call had to be prompted.
texts.4: SP cleared the assigned responsibility airspace completely on every turn, with an unbroken scan cycle that covered No1, the sector and the terrain without any of them lapsing. Safe maneuvering altitude over the mountainous section was assessed ahead of the turn rather than at the roll-in. Clearing calls were made in time for the leader to use them.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the assigned responsibility airspace on every turn but the sector check was brief and came late in the scan cycle, leaving little margin before the roll-in. Terrain clearance over the high ground was confirmed correctly, though only after the turn had been initiated. SP is expected to complete the sector clearing before the maneuver starts and to keep the scan share balanced with the lookout on No1.

texts_at.1: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 before the tactical turns, due to the sector check being brief and coming late in the scan cycle before it was completed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the sector check early in the scan cycle, not brief and late.
texts_at.2: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 before the tactical turns, due to terrain clearance over the high ground being confirmed a beat after the turn had already started. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm terrain clearance before the turn starts, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 before the tactical turns, due to the scan cycle giving the sector a fraction less time than No1 before it was balanced. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to balance the scan share between the sector and No1 from the first cycle.

texts_above.2: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 before and during each tactical turn, according to the relative position in the formation, the scan cycled between No1, the sector of responsibility and the terrain ahead with no clearing call needing to be prompted. Balancing the scan share between the sector and No1 from the first cycle would complete the clearing discipline. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent responsibility-airspace discipline.
texts_above.3: SP executed clearing of the assigned responsibility airspace as No2 on every turn, safe maneuvering altitude over the high ground confirmed correctly before each turn was initiated. The only refinement available was to hold that same early clearing through the busiest reversal of the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined responsibility-airspace discipline.
texts_above.4: SP cleared the assigned responsibility airspace completely on every turn, with an unbroken scan cycle that covered No1, the sector and the terrain without any of them lapsing, safe maneuvering altitude over the mountainous section assessed ahead of the turn rather than at the roll-in with clearing calls made in time for the leader to use them. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless responsibility-airspace discipline.

error_modes.label: Energy management and correction technique to hold position

texts.0: SP, due to corrections applied with bank alone and no conversion of altitude into airspeed, did not exploit the aircraft energy in order to maintain the tactical position. The aircraft ended up slow and aft with no energy available to close, and engine handling ignored the fuel reserve while attempting to catch up at maximum power. The IP had to take control of the correction and rebuild the position.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect choice of correction technique, did not alleviate the deviations from the tactical formation position in a timely manner. Corrections were made with power only where a geometry correction was required, so the position error persisted through the leg and was resolved only after the IP described the technique. Engine use during the catch-up left less fuel reserve than the profile allowed.
texts.2: SP, due to a correction started later than the first indication of the deviation, did not apply the position correction promptly at the first reversal. The correct combination of geometry and power was then selected and the tactical position was recovered before the next turn without intervention. Engine handling stayed consistent with the required fuel reserve.
texts.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical formation position, using altitude and airspeed against each other rather than power alone. Deviations were identified early and the appropriate correction technique was applied in time to prevent them from developing. Engine use remained consistent with the fuel reserve required for the route.
texts.4: SP managed the aircraft energy so precisely that position corrections were anticipated rather than reactive, with altitude and airspeed traded smoothly through every reversal. The technique selected matched each deviation and removed it before it became visible in the formation geometry. Power was used economically and the fuel reserve stayed well ahead of the plan.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the tactical position and applied correct techniques, but corrections were initiated only once the deviation was clearly established rather than at the first indication. The energy trades worked, though several required more power than a timely correction would have needed. SP is expected to recognize the developing deviation earlier and to correct with the smaller energy penalty.

texts_at.1: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical position, due to one correction being started only once the deviation was clearly established rather than at its first indication. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start every correction at the first indication, not once it is clearly established.
texts_at.2: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical position, due to the combination of geometry and power being selected a beat after the first reversal rather than at it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to select the geometry-and-power combination at the first reversal, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical position, due to engine handling being confirmed against the fuel reserve a fraction after the correction rather than with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm engine handling against the fuel reserve with the correction, not a fraction after.

texts_above.2: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical formation position, using altitude and airspeed against each other rather than power alone, deviations identified early with the appropriate correction technique applied in time to prevent them from developing. Confirming engine handling against the fuel reserve with the correction, rather than a fraction after, would trim the energy penalty further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to good energy-management discipline.
texts_above.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to maintain the tactical position, engine use remaining consistent with the fuel reserve required for the route on every correction. The only refinement available was to recognize that same developing deviation a moment earlier still on the fastest reversal. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good energy-management discipline.

error_modes.label: Initiative for safe separation and turn execution per the manual

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to make the knock-it-off call when the briefed parameters were exceeded, did not take the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns. The turn was continued toward a converging flight path with closure that the geometry could not absorb, and it was not executed as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The IP had to call the knock-it-off and take control to open the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to state the deconfliction call while the maneuver was still developing, did not take timely initiative for safe separation. The tactical turn was flown with a sequence that departed from the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the rollout was not in tactical formation position. Separation was restored only after the IP directed the correction and the call.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation at the point where the closure first became apparent, did not make the deconfliction call at the earliest opportunity. The call was made shortly afterwards, the turn was completed as described in the manual and the rollout re-established the tactical position without intervention. Separation was never allowed to reduce beyond the briefed minimum.
texts.3: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns and executed them as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, rolling out in tactical formation position. Deconfliction calls were made in time to be useful to the leader and the flight path was adjusted before closure developed. The sequence of each turn matched the briefed procedure.
texts.4: SP anticipated every deconfliction requirement, calling and adjusting before closure could develop, and executed each tactical turn exactly as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The rollouts placed the aircraft directly in tactical formation position with no further correction. Safety of separation was maintained without any reduction in the accuracy of the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP maintained safe separation and flew the tactical turns to the published procedure, but the deconfliction calls came later than the developing geometry warranted. Separation was never reduced below the briefed minimum, though the margin used was consistently the smallest acceptable. SP is expected to make the call at the first indication of closure rather than after confirming it.

texts_at.1: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, due to the deconfliction call being made only after the closure was confirmed rather than at its first indication. texts_at.3: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, due to the rollout being confirmed in tactical formation position a fraction after the call rather than as part of it. Confirming the rollout position as part of the call, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the initiative further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid separation-initiative discipline.
